subtype: One bad boss means all workplaces [Actor]
passage: I'm Chaitanya, Pradeep's flatmate, and I watched his first job happen. His manager at the logistics firm shouted in meetings, sent messages at midnight, and once tore up Pradeep's report in front of the team. Pradeep came home grey for a year. He quit in March. That part made sense. What I didn't expect was what came after. When his cousin sent him an opening at a small design studio, he said, 'All offices are the same. Every manager is like that.' When I showed him a post from a firm my friend loves working at, he said, 'She's just lucky.' He hasn't applied anywhere in five months. He fixes the neighbours' laptops for cash now and says it's safer. I believe his first job was awful. I'm just not sure it's the whole world.

qa.q: When did Pradeep quit the logistics firm?
qa.a: Pradeep quit in March.

qa.q: Why might 'All offices are the same' feel true to Pradeep?
qa.a: A year of shouting and midnight messages hurt so much that it feels like knowledge about every workplace, and believing it protects Pradeep from risking that pain again.

qa.q: What small step could test Pradeep's conclusion?
qa.a: Pradeep could talk to the friend who loves working at that firm, or apply to the one small studio, to gather evidence from more than one workplace.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Pradeep's decision?
qa.a: Chaitanya accepts that the first job was truly awful but worries the conclusion is bigger than the evidence and is quietly shrinking Pradeep's life.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's eyes, an adult whose real bad first job has turned into a belief that every workplace is toxic, so he stops applying.

passage:
March: Sudha resigned from the call centre after eight months under a supervisor who timed her breaks and mocked her accent in front of the whole floor. Over chai with Tanvir she said, 'Never again. Every office is a cage. They're all like him.'
May: Tanvir forwarded a job at a public library's digital archive. Sudha didn't open the link. 'Same thing with a nicer building.' She spent the afternoon scrolling job sites without applying, her stomach tightening at every 'team player'.
July: Tanvir asked one question. 'How many workplaces have you actually worked in?' Sudha counted. 'One.' She was quiet a long time. 'One really bad one.' That night she opened the library link, read it twice and saved it. It was more than she'd done in four months.

qa.q: How long did Sudha work at the call centre?
qa.a: Sudha worked there for eight months.

qa.q: Why does Sudha's stomach tighten at every 'team player'?
qa.a: Those words remind Sudha of the supervisor, so every new job ad feels like a doorway back into the same cage, and fear speaks louder than the facts.

qa.q: What turning point did Tanvir's question create?
qa.a: Asking how many workplaces Sudha had worked in showed that the conclusion rested on one example, and that night she opened and saved the library job.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tanvir to watch Sudha ignore the links?
qa.a: Tanvir probably feels concerned but patient, believing Sudha deserves a better job, and chooses one careful question over more pushing.

grounding: Shows an adult whose truly bad first job leads her to call every office a cage, until she notices the conclusion rests on one workplace.

subtype: One bad boss means all workplaces [Actor]
passage: Abhinav, you told me yesterday that all managers are the same, so why bother with the interview. Let me tell you about me at twenty-four. My first boss at the printing press was a terror. He counted our tea breaks, cut our pay for a smudged proof, called me 'Yusuf the donkey' in front of the apprentices. I lasted a year. After that I told everyone, 'Offices are prisons. Owners are all the same.' For two years I refused every job and sold phone covers at a stall, telling myself it was freedom. Then a friend dragged me to meet Mr Fernandes, who ran a small publishing house. He asked my opinion on a book cover in the first ten minutes. I nearly cried. I worked for him for eleven years. That first boss was real. My rule about all bosses wasn't.

qa.q: How long did Yusuf work for Mr Fernandes?
qa.a: Yusuf worked for him for eleven years.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf call selling phone covers 'freedom'?
qa.a: After a year of humiliation, avoiding every office felt like safety, so Yusuf renamed the fear as freedom rather than face the risk of another bad boss.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Yusuf's story, and what could Abhinav take from it?
qa.a: Meeting Mr Fernandes, who asked Yusuf's opinion within ten minutes, broke the rule; Abhinav could treat the interview as a chance to meet one more real manager.

qa.q: How might Abhinav hear 'That first boss was real. My rule about all bosses wasn't'?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel understood, since the bad experience is taken seriously, while being gently pushed to question the rule that grew from it.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how a cruel first boss made Yusuf decide all workplaces were prisons, and how one good workplace proved the rule wrong.

subtype: One bad boss means all workplaces [Actor]
passage:
Gautam's savings would last maybe six more weeks. He'd left his first job, as a line cook in a big hotel in Goa, after a head chef who screamed, threw pans and made him work fourteen-hour shifts without a day off for a month.

Now he was back in his parents' flat in Pune, and it had rained for nine days.

His sister Nikita put her phone in front of him. "A small café in Aundh. They want a cook. The owner's a woman who used to be a teacher. Reviews say she's lovely to staff."

"Every kitchen is the same," Gautam said. "They all scream. They all use you. I'm not doing that again."

"You worked in one kitchen."

"One was enough to know."

Nikita left the phone on the table. He didn't touch it. That evening he searched for data-entry jobs he didn't want, because at least they weren't kitchens. The rain kept falling.

qa.q: How long did Gautam's savings last, roughly?
qa.a: Maybe six more weeks.

qa.q: Why does "One was enough to know" feel true to Gautam?
qa.a: His first kitchen was genuinely harsh, so the pain is real, and it seems safer to assume all kitchens are like that. The strong memory makes one example feel like the whole trade.

qa.q: What small step could Gautam take without committing to a new kitchen job?
qa.a: He could visit the café or talk to the owner for ten minutes to see how she treats staff. Checking one more example would test whether every kitchen really is the same.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when Gautam leaves her phone untouched?
qa.a: Nikita might feel frustrated and worried, especially with his savings running low. She clearly wants to help and may feel shut out.

grounding: A young cook with a brutal first job decides every kitchen is toxic and stops trying, when the experience is real but the conclusion outruns it.

subtype: One bad boss means all workplaces [Actor]
passage:
In a café near the Anna Nagar tower park, Rashmi slid her phone across the table to Jeevan. "The school my cousin works at needs a maths teacher. The principal is known for being kind. Apply."

Jeevan didn't even look. "No. All schools are toxic."

"All?"

"You saw what happened at St Paul's. The principal shouted at me in the staff room in front of everyone. Wrote me up for being two minutes late. Made me cover four extra classes a week, unpaid." He stirred his coffee hard. "That's what schools are. I'm done with teaching."

"That was one principal, Jeevan."

"It was a year of my life."

"I know. It was awful. But you loved the kids. You still talk about the Class 8 boy who finally got fractions."

Jeevan was quiet. Then: "They'd all be the same underneath."

Rashmi took her phone back, but she left the principal's name written on a napkin.

qa.q: What was Jeevan written up for at St Paul's?
qa.a: For being two minutes late.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan insist all schools are toxic, even though he loved the kids?
qa.a: His year under a harsh principal was genuinely painful, and deciding every school is the same protects him from being hurt again. The real experience makes the broad conclusion feel like common sense.

qa.q: What would you advise Jeevan to do with the napkin?
qa.a: Keep it and ask the cousin what the principal is really like, or visit for a short chat. One conversation can test whether this school fits his rule.

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel when Jeevan says they'd all be the same underneath?
qa.a: Rashmi might feel a bit helpless but patient, knowing how much the first job hurt him. Leaving the napkin shows she still hopes he'll try.

grounding: A young teacher with a harsh first principal decides all schools are toxic and gives up teaching, a conclusion that goes beyond his one real experience.
